sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**VohuManah** ​(*vohumanah*) — ‌Good Mind, ‌Cattle ​· Good ​thought ​— belongs ​to the ​Zoroastrian ‌tradition, where ​it is ​catalogued ‌under the ​domain ‌"Good Mind, ​Cattle". The ‌name ​means "Good ​thought"[^1].

**VohuManah** ​— ​Good Mind, ​Good ‌Purpose — ​is the ‌first ​of the ‌six Amesha ​Spentas, ‌the Holy ​Immortals ‌who surround ​Ahura Mazdā. ​He ‌is the ‌thought that ‌chooses ​truth before ​word ‌and deed, ​the guardian ​of ‌cattle and ​patient prosperity, ​and ‌the divine ​visitor ‌who appeared ​to Zarathuštra ​on ​the river ​Dāitya to ‌open ‌the way ​to ‌revelation.[^2]

PuniCodex ​records the ​canonical ‌scholarly spelling ‌**VohuManah** and ‌serves ‌its temple ​at ‌[its temple](https://punicodex.com/vohumanah/). ​The displayed ​form ​is ASCII-equivalent ‌— a ​description ​computed from ​the ‌displayed form ​itself. The ​plain ​ASCII form ‌*vohumanah* contains ​the ‌same letters: ​no ‌recovered diacritics ​or special ‌encoding ‌is claimed. ​The work ​here ​is consistent ​citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in ​Avestan as ​**𐬬𐬊𐬵𐬎 ​𐬨𐬀𐬥𐬀𐬵**. Etymologically ​it ​means "Good ‌thought"[^1].

​The ​canonical spelling ‌**VohuManah** ​matches the ‌conventional ​scholarly romanization. ‌The ​plain ​ASCII form ​*vohumanah* ​contains the ​same ‌letters, ​so no ‌lost ​diacritics or ‌encoding ​transition is ‌claimed. ​The ‌editorial work ​is ​to fix ‌one ‌reviewed reference ‌spelling, ​preserve ​capitalization and ‌provenance, ​and keep ​the ‌original ​evidence visible. ​The ‌displayed form ​is ‌ASCII-equivalent — ​a ​description ​computed from ​the ‌displayed form ‌itself.

​The ‌letter-by-letter transformation ​runs:

- ​**v** → ‌**V** ‌— Same, ‌capitalized
- ‌**o** ​→ **o** ‌— ​Same
- **h** ​→ ​**h** — ‌Same
- ​**u** ​→ **u** ​— ‌Same
- **m** ​→ ​**M** ​— Same, ‌capitalized
- ​**a** → ‌**a** ​— Same
- ‌**n** ​→ ‌**n** — ‌Same
- ​**a** → ​**a** ​— Same
- ​**h** ‌→ ‌**h** — ​Same

sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is **/vohumanah/** ​— ​Restored ​scholarly ‌form.

Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ‌**vohumanah** — ​The ‌canonical ​restored ‌form VohuManah.

​For ​the ​modern speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: Read ‌"VohuManah" ​using ‌the reconstructed ​pronunciation ‌above; ​the ‌conventional Latin ​spelling ​adds ‌no diacritic ‌marks.

‌The ​conventional ​spelling "VohuManah" ‌is ​already ​written in ‌Latin ​letters; ​the ‌lowercase form ​"vohumanah" ‌differs ​only ​in capitalization.

​The ​pronunciation ‌given above ‌reconstructs ​the ‌sound ​world in ​which ‌VohuManah ‌was invoked. ‌Modern ‌speakers ​should ‌not expect ​exact ​identity ​with ancient ‌phonology; ​the ​reconstruction ​is a ‌scholarly ​compass, ​not a ​performance ‌prescription. ​The ‌reconstructed pronunciation ​of ‌VohuManah ​is explained ‌separately ‌from ​its ​conventional Latin ​spelling, ​which ‌adds no ‌diacritic ​marks.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The ​stories of ‌VohuManah ‌place ​good mind, ​cattle ​at ​the center ​of ‌a ​living mythological ​world.

### ‌Origins (Myth)

​VohuManah ‌appears ​in zoroastrian ‌tradition ​as ​good mind, ​cattle. ​The ​name's meaning, ‌"Good ​thought", shapes ‌the ​narratives ‌told about ​this ‌figure.

### ​Worship and ‌Memory ​(Cult)

​Devotees and ‌later ‌tradition-keepers preserved ‌VohuManah ​in ​ritual, text, ‌and ​iconography, ​ensuring the ‌name ​survived ​into the ‌modern ​scholarly record.

‌The ​myths ​of VohuManah ​survive ​in ‌fragments, summaries, ‌and ​later ‌retellings. Each ​version ​reflects the ‌interests ‌of ‌its tellers ‌— ​poets, ‌priests, philosophers, ​and ​scholars. ​The PuniCodex ‌entry ​does not ​privilege ​a ‌single version; ​it ​gathers ​the attestations ‌so ​that ‌readers can ​compare ‌them. The ​restoration ‌VohuManah ‌gives the ​figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or artifact ​in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is yet ​assigned ​to ‌VohuManah ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence should ​be ​read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Zoroastrian name ​of ‌this ​type ‌the ​material ‌record is ​expected ‌to ​be ​thin, ‌and ‌the ‌primary evidence ​remains ​the ‌textual ​testimony ​gathered ‌in the ​Scholarly ​Sources ‌section.

​Were ‌such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ​would ‌take ‌recognizable ​forms: votive ‌or ​dedicatory ​inscriptions ‌naming ‌𐬬𐬊𐬵𐬎 ‌𐬨𐬀𐬥𐬀𐬵, ‌sanctuary or ​cult ‌remains ​tied ​to ​good ‌mind and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional ​attributes ​(name and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be ‌weighed ​against the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name ​before entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body: Cattle ​are ‌the ‌clue. Vohu ​Manah's ​charge ​is ​not ​intellect ‌but the ​slow, ​warm, ‌patient ​goods: ‌herds, ​harvests, the ‌long ​prosperity ​of ​a ​well-kept ​household. The ‌Good ​Mind ‌is ​the ‌mindset of ​the ‌good ​shepherd ‌— ​unhurried, ​watchful, kind ‌to ‌what ‌feeds ​us. ​Against ‌it stands ​Aka ​Manah, ‌the ​mind ​that ‌is clever, ​quick, ‌and ​ruinous. ​The ​pair ​maps uncomfortably ‌well ‌onto ​our ‌own ​economy ​of attention: ‌the ‌feed ‌engineered ‌to ​be ‌bad for ​us ​is ​a ‌cattle-drive ​run by ​Aka ​Manah. ‌Zarathuštra's ​question ​— ​whose mind ‌are ​you ‌thinking ​with? ‌— ​is four ‌millennia ‌old ​and ​still ​the ​diagnostic question ‌of ‌a ​life.[^1]
